patient.name: Doreen Fitzgerald
patient.setting: GP surgery, then upper GI surgical clinic
patient.complaint: Fullness after small meals, vomiting after eating and tiredness for 4 months
background: COPD with a chronic cough; ex-smoker
Lives alone in Bermondsey; retired seamstress

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' where you must tell a sliding hernia (reflux, worse lying down) from a rolling para-oesophageal hernia (early satiety, post-prandial vomiting, minimal reflux), or spot a complication such as volvulus or Cameron ulcers.

points: Doreen, 76, feels **full after a few mouthfuls**.
**Vomits** sometimes after meals; heavy pressure behind the breastbone after eating.
Increasingly **tired and breathless** on the stairs.

steps.lead: Hiatus hernias cause reflux, dysphagia, belching and symptoms after big meals or bending. Doreen has the after-meal symptoms but little reflux.

visual.title: Where Doreen feels the pressure
visual.caption: Epigastric and lower retrosternal fullness after meals, from stomach trapped in the chest.

steps.text: The abdomen itself is soft and non-tender.

steps.lead: Early satiety, vomiting after meals, retrosternal pressure, **minimal reflux** and a slow onset: Doreen fits a **para-oesophageal (rolling)** hernia.
Part of Doreen's stomach has pushed through the **oesophageal hiatus** into her chest.

steps.q: Doreen has early satiety and vomiting after meals but almost no heartburn. Which type is it most likely to be?
o: Mixed type with GOJ in the chest
steps.r: With the GOJ still below the diaphragm there is **minimal reflux**; the trapped fundus causes fullness and vomiting.

steps.lead: Doreen is over 50, obese, coughs every day from COPD and strains with constipation: constant **raised intra-abdominal pressure**.
Doreen's tiredness may be **Cameron ulcers** bleeding slowly; her hernia could also twist (**volvulus**) or strangulate.
Doreen's **amlodipine** relaxes the LOS and can worsen reflux, so it is a drug to review.

steps.text: Do not assume all hiatus hernias present with heartburn. A **rolling** hernia often has **minimal reflux**; early satiety and vomiting are the clue.

investigation.exam: Expect a question on the most sensitive test (barium swallow), the gold standard (OGD, urgent if red flags) or the chest X-ray finding (retrocardiac gas-filled structure).

steps.r: **Red flags** (anaemia, vomiting, age) mean urgent OGD to exclude cancer and find the source of bleeding.

steps.lead: Doreen's **OGD** shows a large para-oesophageal hernia with linear **Cameron erosions** at the diaphragmatic pinch, and no tumour.

visual.caption: Rounded retrocardiac opacity containing a gas bubble: stomach in the chest.

steps.text: The 'mass' behind the heart is gas-filled stomach, not a tumour.

steps.lead: Doreen's **chest X-ray** shows a retrocardiac gas bubble; a **barium swallow** maps the hernia best before surgery.
Before her repair, Doreen has **manometry** and **24-hour pH monitoring** to check oesophageal function and reflux.

steps.text: A retrocardiac 'mass' with an air-fluid level is a **hiatus hernia** until proven otherwise, not a lung tumour.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' where the type decides: sliding gets lifestyle plus PPI (Nissen fundoplication if refractory), rolling gets surgical repair, and any volvulus, obstruction or bleed gets urgent surgical referral.

steps.title: Managing a hiatus hernia
nodes: Review drugs that relax the LOS

steps.lead: If Doreen's had been a **sliding** hernia, she would start with **lifestyle advice** and a **PPI** for 4–8 weeks.

steps.q: Doreen has a symptomatic rolling hernia with Cameron ulcers. What is first-line treatment?
steps.r: Rolling hernias risk **volvulus, obstruction and strangulation**, so surgical repair is first-line.

steps.lead: Doreen is booked for **laparoscopic hernia reduction and repair with fundoplication**. Her amlodipine is swapped for another antihypertensive.

points: While waiting: oral iron and a PPI to heal the erosions.
Safety-net: sudden chest or epigastric pain, retching without vomiting.
Told to call 999 rather than wait for clinic.

steps.lead: If Doreen's hernia twisted, bled or obstructed, she would need an **urgent surgical referral**, not a clinic appointment.

steps.text: Do not just discharge a **rolling** hernia on a PPI. That is the plan for sliding hernias; rolling ones need surgical assessment.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why a sliding hernia causes reflux but a rolling one does not, why raised abdominal pressure causes herniation, why Cameron ulcers cause anaemia and how a Nissen fundoplication works.

steps.lead: In Doreen, stomach has crossed from abdomen to thorax through the **oesophageal hiatus**.
Doreen's GOJ is still fixed below the diaphragm, so her barrier works and she has **little reflux**, but her rolling hernia can **strangulate**.

steps.title: Why a sliding hernia causes reflux
nodes: GOJ slides up through the hiatus
Diaphragmatic crura no longer squeeze the LOS

steps.lead: Doreen's obesity, COPD cough and straining push the stomach up and **widen her hiatus**.

steps.lead: Doreen's anaemia comes from **Cameron ulcers**: erosions where the diaphragm pinches the herniated stomach, oozing blood for months.

steps.q: Why did Doreen's Cameron ulcers cause microcytic anaemia?
steps.r: Slow **occult bleeding** drains iron stores, giving **iron deficiency** (microcytic) anaemia.

steps.lead: Doreen's **fundoplication** wraps her fundus around the lower oesophagus, rebuilding the anti-reflux barrier after the repair.

mcq.q: Which is the most common type of hiatus hernia?
In a rolling hernia, where is the gastro-oesophageal junction?
mcq.r: The GOJ **stays below the diaphragm**; the fundus rolls up beside the oesophagus.

mcq.q: Which drug should be avoided because it relaxes the LOS?
mcq.r: **Calcium channel blockers** such as amlodipine relax the LOS.
**Linear erosions** at the diaphragmatic pinch of a hiatus hernia, causing anaemia.

mcq.q: Which complication is a particular risk of rolling hernias?
What is the most sensitive diagnostic investigation for hiatus hernia?
mcq.r: **Barium swallow**; OGD is the gold standard, urgent if red flags.

mcq.q: What can a chest X-ray show in hiatus hernia?
mcq.r: A **rounded retrocardiac structure with a stomach bubble**.

mcq.q: What is first-line management of a rolling hiatus hernia?
mcq.r: **Surgical repair** with fundoplication because of volvulus and strangulation risk.

mcq.q: Which operation is used for a sliding hernia when PPI and lifestyle fail?
Which ligament weakens in a sliding hiatus hernia?
mcq.r: The **phrenico-oesophageal ligament**, letting the GOJ slide up.

technique.stem: A 79 year old woman has a 5 month history of fullness after small meals, intermittent vomiting after eating and a heavy pressure behind her sternum after meals. She has very little heartburn. She is obese and has a chronic cough. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Upper GI diagnosis: is reflux the main symptom or not?

clues: pressure behind her sternum after meals
obese and has a chronic cough
steps.x: Early satiety, post-prandial vomiting, retrosternal pressure, **minimal reflux**, raised abdominal pressure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Para-oesophageal (rolling) hiatus hernia**.

elim: No weight loss, mass or anaemia given; slow post-prandial symptoms fit a hernia.
GORD would be dominated by heartburn.
Peptic ulcer gives epigastric pain, not early satiety with minimal pain.
A sliding hernia presents with reflux.

steps.x: **C. Para-oesophageal hernia.** Fullness + vomiting + minimal reflux = rolling.

technique.stem: A 72 year old man has early satiety and post-prandial retrosternal discomfort. He has no heartburn. He has a chest X-ray because of a chronic cough. His lungs are clear on examination, and he has a large para-oesophageal hiatus hernia on a previous barium study.
technique.q: Which is the most likely finding on his chest X-ray?

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' on imaging.
Known rolling hernia; stomach sits behind the heart.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Rounded retrocardiac structure with a gas bubble** or air-fluid level.

elim: Hilar nodes suggest sarcoid or lymphoma.
Free air means perforation.
Lungs are clear on examination.
A widened mediastinum suggests dissection or nodes.

steps.x: **C. Retrocardiac gas-filled structure.** Stomach in the chest.

technique.stem: An 81 year old woman with a known rolling hiatus hernia has 3 hours of sudden severe epigastric and chest pain. She keeps retching but cannot vomit. A nasogastric tube cannot be passed. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. ECG and troponin are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral omeprazole and review in 2 weeks

steps.x: Emergency management: decide how urgent.

clues: sudden severe epigastric and chest pain
steps.x: **Borchardt's triad**: gastric volvulus, with shock. Cardiac cause excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Resuscitate and **urgent surgical referral**.

elim: Discharge would miss a strangulating stomach.
Medical treatment does not untwist a volvulus.
Outpatient imaging is far too slow.
A routine scope delays emergency surgery.

steps.x: **E. Urgent surgical referral.** Volvulus, ischaemia or obstruction = surgeon now.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man has a sliding hiatus hernia. He has a BMI of 38, a chronic cough from COPD and long-standing constipation with straining. He asks why he developed the hernia.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Chronic pressure widens the diaphragmatic hiatus

steps.x: A mechanism: link his risk factors to herniation.
Three causes of **raised intra-abdominal pressure**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Raised pressure pushes the stomach up and **widens the hiatus**.

elim: Acid does not change the anatomy of the hiatus.
The LOS is weakened, not hypertrophied.
Slow emptying is not the cause of herniation.
Vagal damage is not the mechanism.

steps.x: **A. Pressure widens the hiatus.** Obesity, pregnancy and chronic cough all do this.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man has 6 months of heartburn and acid regurgitation after large meals, worse when he lies flat or bends to tie his shoes. He belches frequently. He is obese. Endoscopy shows the gastro-oesophageal junction 4 cm above the diaphragmatic pinch.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Reflux worse lying or bending, with the GOJ displaced above the diaphragm, is a sliding hiatus hernia. In a rolling hernia the GOJ stays below the diaphragm.

steps.x: Which hernia, or another oesophageal problem?

clues: worse when he lies flat or bends
gastro-oesophageal junction 4 cm above the diaphragmatic pinch
steps.x: Reflux-dominant symptoms; **GOJ moved up**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sliding hiatus hernia**.

elim: Achalasia causes dysphagia to solids and liquids.
In a rolling hernia the GOJ stays below the diaphragm.
A stricture causes dysphagia, not this endoscopic finding.
A pouch causes regurgitation of old food and halitosis.

steps.x: **E. Sliding hiatus hernia.** GOJ up = sliding = reflux.

practice.stem: A 77 year old woman has 4 months of early satiety, vomiting after meals and post-prandial retrosternal pressure. She has minimal heartburn. She is obese. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Rounded retrocardiac opacity with an air-fluid level.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Early satiety, post-prandial vomiting and pressure with minimal reflux, plus a retrocardiac gas-filled structure, is a rolling (para-oesophageal) hernia.

steps.x: Upper GI diagnosis with an X-ray.
Rolling-hernia symptoms; stomach behind the heart on the film.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Para-oesophageal (rolling) hernia**.

elim: Achalasia gives a dilated oesophagus and dysphagia to liquids.
No weight loss or anaemia, and the X-ray shows stomach above the diaphragm.
A pouch sits in the neck.
A sliding hernia presents with reflux.

steps.x: **C. Para-oesophageal hiatus hernia.** Minimal reflux + retrocardiac bubble.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man has post-prandial fullness and occasional vomiting with little heartburn. A chest X-ray showed a retrocardiac opacity. He has a barium swallow to define the anatomy before surgery. The gastro-oesophageal junction is in its normal position.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on the barium swallow?
practice.e: In a rolling hernia barium shows the gastric fundus herniated above the diaphragm alongside the oesophagus, with the GOJ in place. Bird's beak is achalasia; apple-core is cancer.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' on barium.

clues: gastro-oesophageal junction is in its normal position
steps.x: Rolling hernia: GOJ below, fundus up.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Fundus above the diaphragm** beside the oesophagus.

elim: Apple-core is a malignant stricture.
Bird's beak is achalasia.
Corkscrew is diffuse oesophageal spasm.
A pouch is in the pharynx, with halitosis.

steps.x: **D. Gastric fundus above the diaphragm.** Barium is the most sensitive test.

practice.stem: An 80 year old woman with a large hiatus hernia has 3 months of fatigue and breathlessness on exertion. She has no melaena or haematemesis and takes no NSAIDs. Upper GI endoscopy shows linear erosions on the gastric folds at the level of the diaphragm, and no tumour.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
practice.e: Linear erosions at the diaphragmatic pinch of a hiatus hernia are Cameron ulcers; chronic occult bleeding causes iron deficiency anaemia.

steps.x: The cause of anaemia in a hernia patient.

clues: linear erosions on the gastric folds at the level of the diaphragm
steps.x: Occult bleeding from erosions at the pinch point; labs show iron deficiency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cameron ulcers**.

elim: Angiodysplasia is vascular, mostly in the right colon.
Coeliac causes malabsorption, not visible gastric erosions.
OGD shows no tumour.
Varices need portal hypertension and present with big bleeds.

steps.x: **B. Cameron ulcers.** Hernia + erosions at the diaphragm + microcytic anaemia.

practice.stem: A 78 year old woman with a known para-oesophageal hiatus hernia has 2 hours of sudden severe epigastric pain. She is retching but cannot vomit, and a nasogastric tube cannot be passed. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Severe epigastric pain, unproductive retching and failure to pass an NG tube (Borchardt's triad) in a rolling hernia is gastric volvulus. A raised lactate suggests ischaemia.

steps.x: Acute complication of a known rolling hernia.
**Borchardt's triad**; normal troponin and amylase, high lactate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Gastric volvulus**.

elim: Troponin is normal.
Amylase is normal.
Boerhaave follows forceful vomiting; she cannot vomit.
Perforation gives peritonitis and free air, not failed NG passage.

steps.x: **D. Gastric volvulus.** Rolling hernias twist.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man with a sliding hiatus hernia has had well-controlled reflux on lifestyle measures. Six weeks ago his GP started a new antihypertensive and his heartburn has worsened since. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. He has no new red flag symptoms.
practice.q: Which drug is most likely to have worsened his symptoms?
practice.e: Calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine relax the lower oesophageal sphincter and worsen reflux, so they should be avoided in hiatus hernia and GORD.

steps.x: A drug precipitant of reflux.
A new BP drug that relaxes smooth muscle.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Amlodipine** (calcium channel blocker).

elim: Atorvastatin is not an antihypertensive.
Beta-blockers do not typically relax the LOS.
Thiazide-like diuretics cause electrolyte problems, not reflux.
ACE inhibitors cause a dry cough, not heartburn.

steps.x: **A. Amlodipine.** CCBs relax the LOS.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman has post-prandial fullness and regurgitation, worse when bending forward. She has no weight loss, anaemia or dysphagia. A hiatus hernia is suspected and the team want the most sensitive test to demonstrate it.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: A barium swallow is the most sensitive investigation for demonstrating a hiatus hernia. pH monitoring and manometry are additional tests of reflux and motility.

steps.x: It asks for the **most sensitive** test for the hernia.

clues: no weight loss, anaemia or dysphagia
steps.x: No red flags; they want the hernia shown.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Barium swallow**.

elim: pH monitoring measures reflux, not anatomy.
Ultrasound cannot see the hiatus well.
CT can show large hernias but is not the most sensitive first test.
Manometry measures pressures and is additional.

steps.x: **C. Barium swallow.** Most sensitive; OGD is gold standard.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man with a known small sliding hiatus hernia has 2 months of new difficulty swallowing solids and 5 kg weight loss. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: Red flags (dysphagia, weight loss, anaemia) in a hiatus hernia patient mandate urgent endoscopy, the gold standard, to exclude malignancy.

steps.x: Red flags change the test.
Dysphagia and weight loss; anaemia on labs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent OGD**.

elim: Barium cannot biopsy.
CT stages, it does not diagnose.
Manometry is for motility, not red flags.
A breath test ignores the red flags.

steps.x: **D. Upper GI endoscopy.** Red flags = urgent scope.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman has heartburn after large meals, worse lying down. Endoscopy shows a small sliding hiatus hernia with mild oesophagitis and no red flags. She has a BMI of 31, drinks a lot of coffee and eats late.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Uncomplicated sliding hernia is managed with lifestyle advice (weight loss, smaller earlier meals, less caffeine) and a PPI for 4–8 weeks. Surgery is for failed medical treatment.

steps.x: Initial management, and the type is **sliding**.
Small, uncomplicated, modifiable triggers.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lifestyle plus PPI**.

elim: Nissen is for PPI and lifestyle failure.
NG decompression is for volvulus or obstruction.
Surgery is not first-line for a small sliding hernia.
No emergency features.

steps.x: **B. Lifestyle advice and omeprazole.**

practice.stem: A 73 year old woman has a symptomatic para-oesophageal hiatus hernia with early satiety and post-prandial vomiting. She is otherwise fit. There are no signs of volvulus or obstruction today.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Rolling hernias carry a risk of volvulus, obstruction and strangulation, so first-line treatment is surgical repair: laparoscopic hernia reduction and repair with fundoplication.

steps.x: Management: the **type** of hernia decides.

clues: no signs of volvulus or obstruction today
steps.x: Rolling, symptomatic, fit; not an emergency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Elective **laparoscopic repair with fundoplication**.

elim: Dilatation treats strictures or achalasia.
Acid suppression does not stop a rolling hernia twisting.
Lifestyle alone leaves the volvulus risk.
A PPI is the sliding hernia plan.

steps.x: **C. Laparoscopic repair.** Rolling = surgery first-line.

practice.stem: A 49 year old man with a sliding hiatus hernia has persistent reflux despite 6 months of lifestyle changes and high-dose PPI. Endoscopy shows oesophagitis and no Barrett's, and pH monitoring confirms acid reflux. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: When PPI and lifestyle fail in a sliding hiatus hernia, refer for laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication, which wraps the fundus around the lower oesophagus.

steps.x: Next step after medical failure.

clues: despite 6 months of lifestyle changes and high-dose PPI
steps.x: Proven refractory reflux from a sliding hernia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Nissen fundoplication**.

elim: Stents palliate malignant obstruction.
Heller myotomy treats achalasia.
Gastrectomy is for gastric cancer.
Oesophagectomy is for oesophageal cancer.

steps.x: **D. Nissen fundoplication.** Sliding + PPI failure = wrap.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman has heartburn worse lying flat. Barium swallow shows the gastro-oesophageal junction displaced 5 cm above the diaphragm, with the upper stomach in the chest. Rolling hernias also occur but rarely cause reflux.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying mechanism of her hernia?
o: Achalasia of the lower oesophageal sphincter
Fixation of the GOJ below the diaphragm
Herniation of the fundus through a separate defect
practice.e: In a sliding hernia the phrenico-oesophageal ligament weakens, the GOJ slides up and the anti-reflux barrier is lost. A fixed GOJ with a separate defect is a rolling hernia.

steps.x: Mechanism of a **sliding** hernia.

clues: gastro-oesophageal junction displaced 5 cm above the diaphragm
steps.x: GOJ moved up with reflux: sliding.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Phrenico-oesophageal ligament weakens**.

elim: Achalasia is failure of LOS relaxation, not herniation.
A fixed GOJ describes rolling hernias.
A separate defect is the rolling mechanism.
Acid output does not create a hernia.

steps.x: **E. Phrenico-oesophageal ligament weakening.** The GOJ slides; the barrier fails.

glossary.hiatus hernia: Part of the stomach pushed up through the diaphragm's oesophageal opening into the chest.
glossary.oesophageal hiatus: The opening in the diaphragm through which the oesophagus passes.
glossary.sliding hiatus hernia: Commonest type: the GOJ and upper stomach slide up into the chest, causing reflux.
glossary.para-oesophageal: Beside the oesophagus; a rolling hernia where the fundus herniates alongside it.
glossary.rolling hernia: Para-oesophageal hernia: fundus rolls up beside the oesophagus, GOJ stays below the diaphragm.
glossary.GOJ: Gastro-oesophageal junction, where the oesophagus meets the stomach.
glossary.fundus: The dome-shaped top part of the stomach.
glossary.LOS: Lower oesophageal sphincter, the muscle ring that stops reflux.
glossary.GORD: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: acid flowing back into the oesophagus causing symptoms.
glossary.early satiety: Feeling full after eating only a little.
glossary.intra-abdominal pressure: Pressure inside the abdomen, raised by obesity, pregnancy, cough and straining.
glossary.phrenico-oesophageal ligament: Connective tissue anchoring the oesophagus to the diaphragm; weakens in sliding hernias.
glossary.diaphragmatic crura: Muscle bands of the diaphragm that encircle the hiatus and squeeze the LOS.
glossary.gastric volvulus: Twisting of the stomach, causing obstruction and ischaemia; a surgical emergency.
glossary.Borchardt's triad: Severe epigastric pain, retching without vomiting and inability to pass an NG tube: gastric volvulus.
glossary.strangulation: Blood supply to herniated tissue is cut off.
glossary.Cameron ulcers: Linear erosions in a hiatus hernia at the diaphragmatic pinch, causing occult bleeding.
glossary.occult blood loss: Bleeding too slow to be seen, detected by anaemia or tests.
glossary.iron deficiency anaemia: Low haemoglobin with small red cells from lack of iron, often from chronic bleeding.
glossary.amlodipine: Calcium channel blocker for blood pressure that relaxes the LOS and worsens reflux.
glossary.calcium channel blockers: Drugs that relax smooth muscle, including the LOS.
glossary.barium swallow: X-ray after swallowing barium contrast; most sensitive test for hiatus hernia.
glossary.double hump: Barium appearance of two gas-filled bulges, stomach above and below the diaphragm.
glossary.retrocardiac: Behind the heart on a chest X-ray.
glossary.OGD: Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy: camera examination of the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum.
glossary.oesophageal manometry: Pressure measurement along the oesophagus to assess muscle and sphincter function.
glossary.24-hour pH monitoring: Probe measuring oesophageal acid exposure over a day.
glossary.PPI: Proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole; reduces stomach acid.
glossary.antacids: Alkaline medicines that neutralise stomach acid.
glossary.Nissen fundoplication: Operation wrapping the gastric fundus 360 degrees around the lower oesophagus to stop reflux.
glossary.laparoscopic: Keyhole surgery through small abdominal incisions.
glossary.NG tube: Nasogastric tube passed through the nose into the stomach.
